claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by a narrow temperature-time window.
The optimal temperature-time window permits traversal of a single-phase region.
High configurational entropy and balanced interfacial energies overcome inherent segregation tendencies in that window.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneous precursor mixture containing compounds of five to eight noble-metal elements.
A soak at approximately 1100–1200°C with a tailored hold time will access the predicted single-phase region.
Enhanced rapid quenching or structure-directing agents will mitigate sintering.
Uniform heating followed by rapid cooling will lock in a homogeneous alloy phase.
Balanced interfacial and surface energies at elevated temperature promote unified atomic mixing.
Balanced interfacial and surface energies minimize kinetic phase separation.
At the optimal temperature and hold time, configurational entropy overcomes elemental differences by reducing interfacial-energy differences.
Operating outside the optimal temperature-time window causes insufficient mixing and phase separation.
Excessive temperature or hold time can cause uncontrolled morphology or sintering that reduces catalytic surface exposure.
Relative to the baseline, the controlled soak will produce a more uniform elemental distribution and less phase segregation.
The controlled soak and quench will preserve high surface area relative to the baseline.
Synthesis lacking well-defined temperature-time control typically produces mixed phases, elemental segregation, and variable morphology because atomic interdiffusion is unsynchronized.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble metal-based systems containing more than five elements when a single-phase region exists in the free-energy landscape.
The mechanism may not apply to very-low-melting-point systems or systems in which sintering dominates microstructure development.
Optimal temperatures and hold times vary with precursor composition and reactor conditions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism groups both excessively short and excessively long hold times under 'insufficient mixing,' while the intervention separately treats excessive thermal exposure primarily as a sintering risk. Long holds may cause sintering without constituting insufficient mixing, so the stated failure pathway is internally imprecise.
